>Introduction
text.formatted: <head n="1." >Introduction</head>

text.text: Type A. A person says plainly that they do not want more schooling and do not want a promotion.
They do not present this as a temporary lapse or as a problem to be solved.
They accept the costs: lower income, slower advancement, the puzzlement of relatives.
Observers often respond with respect, though not necessarily with admiration.
Type B. A person repeatedly says they will study, get fit, and change their life.
They announce the intention, describe the plan, and express frustration at not having started.
Their daily conduct does not change.
When the distance is pointed out, they explain it by circumstances: too busy, too tired, bad timing, an unsupportive environment.
Observers often respond with irritation, and sometimes with contempt.
Both are types, constructed to isolate a contrast.
The two reactions are familiar from everyday life, and Section 5 turns them into propositions that can fail.
In Type A, the person falls short of what convention expects and is respected.
In Type B, the person holds conventionally desirable aspirations and is held in contempt.
If interpersonal evaluation tracked achievement, Type A should fare worse than Type B, or no better.
Neither has attained much by conventional standards, and Type B at least holds the expected goals.
If evaluation tracked the desirability of goals, Type B should fare better, because study, health, and self-improvement are widely endorsed.
Neither expectation holds.
The contrast suggests that observers register something else.
In both cases there is a distance between conduct and an aspiration that the observer holds the person to.
In Type B the person stated the aspiration.
In Type A convention supplies it.
What differs is how the person stands toward the distance.
The person in Type A answers for it.
The person in Type B places it outside the self.
What in the observer's judgment tracks the actor's stance toward the gap between an aspiration and conduct?
And does it do so whatever the desirability of the aspiration and whether or not it is reached?
This paper proposes gap ownership as the construct that answers the question.
Gap ownership is the actor's expressed stance toward the gap between conduct and an aspiration the observer holds the actor to.
The paper defines three ideal types of this stance: the owned gap, the disowned gap, and the dissolved gap.
The core claim is conditional.
For a fixed gap, observers' evaluations depend on the perceived stance, whatever the desirability of the aspiration and whether or not it is reached.
The paper makes four contributions.
First, it identifies self-regarding aspirations as a domain with its own rule.
Research on hypocrisy concerns moral standing, and research on excuses concerns obligations to other people.
In both, an account is addressed to someone who was wronged.
Study, health, and work aspirations wrong nobody when they are unmet.
The paper predicts that in this domain the usual advantage of a good excuse disappears and that answering for the gap earns more respect.
Second, it separates ownership from false signaling.
False-signaling accounts explain condemnation when an actor has sent a misleading signal about their own conduct.
Ownership is claimed to matter when no public claim was made and no gain is possible.
The paper grounds this claim in the Schutzian argument that habits limit choice (Etzrodt, 2024b).
text.formatted: The paper grounds this claim in the Schutzian argument that habits limit choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Etzrodt, 2024b)</ref>.

text.text: Third, it differentiates the evaluations.
Using Darwall's (1977) two kinds of respect, it separates respect from admiration.
text.formatted: Using <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Darwall's (1977)</ref> two kinds of respect, it separates respect from admiration.

text.text: Using work on contempt, it separates irritation from contempt.
It adds a fourth response, discounting, in which the observer stops treating the person's talk as evidence.
Discounting is a judgment of credibility, where the other three are judgments of the person's standing.
Fourth, it derives the three types from one conceptual pair.
Etzrodt (2024a) reads Durkheimian anomie and Marxian alienation as opposites.
Applied to aspiration and conduct, the pair yields two distinct failures of ownership and predicts that observers answer them differently.
Each proposition derived from the types is stated with the observation that would refute it.
Section 2 identifies what existing accounts explain and where they stop.
Section 3 specifies the construct.
Section 4 proposes mechanisms.
Section 5 states propositions, rival predictions, and boundary conditions.
Section 6 discusses contributions, scope, and a design.
Section 7 returns to the two cases.
This section identifies the explanatory reach of each body of work with respect to the question.
Prior work has studied word-deed inconsistency closely.
The specific object here is different: an observer's judgment of an actor's stance toward a gap in a non-moral aspiration.
Behavioral integrity is the perceived pattern of alignment between an actor's words and deeds (Simons, 2002).
text.formatted: Behavioral integrity is the perceived pattern of alignment between an actor's words and deeds <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Simons, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: The construct belongs to the observer, which is an important precedent.
Its usual object is the manager who espouses values or makes promises, and its usual outcome is trust.
False-signaling research comes closer to the present problem. Jordan et al. (2017) studied people who condemn a behavior that they engage in themselves.
text.formatted: False-signaling research comes closer to the present problem. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Jordan et al. (2017)</ref> studied people who condemn a behavior that they engage in themselves.

text.text: They argue that such condemnation sends a false signal about the condemner's own conduct.
In their fourth study, "honest hypocrites" who admitted to the behavior they condemned were not perceived negatively, although their actions contradicted their stated values.
This is direct evidence that the actor's stance toward the distance matters.
The object, however, is moral condemnation, and the mechanism is a misleading signal sent to an audience. Effron et al. (2018b) integrate these lines.
text.formatted: The object, however, is moral condemnation, and the mechanism is a misleading signal sent to an audience. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Effron et al. (2018b)</ref> integrate these lines.

text.text: In their model, audiences react negatively when they perceive low behavioral integrity and interpret it as a claim to an undeserved moral benefit.
The cultural evidence points the same way.

A misdeed that contradicted preached values drew weaker condemnation in Indonesia, India, and Japan than in the United States (Effron et al., 2018a). Zhao and Watamura (2025) replicated the main false-signaling comparisons with a Japanese sample and found that Japanese participants drew the line between liars and hypocrites differently.
text.formatted: A misdeed that contradicted preached values drew weaker condemnation in Indonesia, India, and Japan than in the United States <ref type="bibr">(Effron et al., 2018a)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Zhao and Watamura (2025)</ref> replicated the main false-signaling comparisons with a Japanese sample and found that Japanese participants drew the line between liars and hypocrites differently.

text.text: Studies of the lay concept point the same way. Alicke et al. (2013) asked which features of a scenario lead people to call an actor a hypocrite.
text.formatted: Studies of the lay concept point the same way. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Alicke et al. (2013)</ref> asked which features of a scenario lead people to call an actor a hypocrite.

text.text: The features included weakness of will and whether the attitude was stated publicly. Laurent and Clark (2019) conclude that hypocrisy is perceived as strongest when attitudes are publicly imposed on others in an attempt to appear morally superior.
text.formatted: The features included weakness of will and whether the attitude was stated publicly. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Laurent and Clark (2019)</ref> conclude that hypocrisy is perceived as strongest when attitudes are publicly imposed on others in an attempt to appear morally superior.

text.text: A private, self-regarding aspiration that goes unmet lies far from this prototype.
Where this stops: the object is moral standing, and the trigger is a signal or a claim to moral benefit.
The actor's acknowledgment enters as an experimental condition.
It is not yet a construct with its own types. Darwall (1977) distinguishes two kinds of respect.
text.formatted: It is not yet a construct with its own types. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Darwall (1977)</ref> distinguishes two kinds of respect.

text.text: Recognition respect is a disposition to weigh some feature of its object appropriately in deliberation and to act accordingly, and it is the respect owed to all persons as persons.
Appraisal respect is a positive appraisal of a person, either as a person or as engaged in some pursuit, and it comes in degrees (Darwall, 1977, p. 38).
text.formatted: Appraisal respect is a positive appraisal of a person, either as a person or as engaged in some pursuit, and it comes in degrees <ref type="bibr">(Darwall, 1977, p. 38)</ref>.

text.text: The present problem needs this distinction.
The puzzle in Type A is that the person is respected without being admired.
Darwall's distinction is normative.
It does not say which cues in ordinary talk lead an observer to grant respect to a person whose goals the observer does not share.
One empirical line comes close. Bellezza et al. (2014) studied people who visibly depart from a norm, for example by wearing gym clothes in a luxury shop.
text.formatted: One empirical line comes close. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bellezza et al. (2014)</ref> studied people who visibly depart from a norm, for example by wearing gym clothes in a luxury shop.

text.text: Observers credited them with higher status and competence.
The effect is mediated by perceived autonomy, and it disappears when the departure is depicted as unintentional.
Deliberateness is thus the active ingredient.
The outcome in that work is status and competence, which are appraisals of merit.
The cue is dress and other visible conduct, where the present paper studies the actor's account of a shortfall.
Where this stops: no account of how a person's talk about their own shortfalls feeds the observer's respect.
For Fischer and Giner-Sorolla (2016), contempt arises when a person's character is appraised as bad and unresponsive to change.
text.formatted: For <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Fischer and Giner-Sorolla (2016)</ref>, contempt arises when a person's character is appraised as bad and unresponsive to change.

text.text: It leads to attempts at social exclusion. Hutcherson and Gross (2011) show that contempt differs from anger and disgust in its antecedents and consequences.
text.formatted: It leads to attempts at social exclusion. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hutcherson and Gross (2011)</ref> show that contempt differs from anger and disgust in its antecedents and consequences.

text.text: They also find a role for contempt in judging incompetent actions.

If contempt concerns unresponsiveness to change, then a gap that is disowned again and again is a plausible trigger. Miceli and Castelfranchi (2018), writing in this journal, describe contempt as an emotion of disrespect.
text.formatted: If contempt concerns unresponsiveness to change, then a gap that is disowned again and again is a plausible trigger. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Miceli and Castelfranchi (2018)</ref>, writing in this journal, describe contempt as an emotion of disrespect.

text.text: It implies a sense of superiority over the target and pessimistic feelings about the target's possibility of betterment.
The second component matters here, because a gap that is disowned again and again gives observers grounds for that pessimism.
The antecedents in this literature are general.
The gap between aspiration and conduct is not the studied trigger.
Irritation, the milder response, is not specified as a distinct evaluation with its own conditions.
Where this stops: the gap is not the object, and the step from irritation to contempt is not specified.
Research on the intention-behavior gap documents the shortfall between what people intend and what they do.
It also identifies the conditions under which intentions are realized (Sheeran, 2002; Sheeran & Webb, 2016).
text.formatted: It also identifies the conditions under which intentions are realized <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Sheeran, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Sheeran & Webb, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This literature explains why gaps arise.
Its dependent variable is the actor's behavior.

Philosophy calls a related problem akrasia, acting against one's better judgment, and this journal has treated it from the social side. Romaioli et al. (2008) propose that akrasia is a narrative configuration generated by an observer who is engaged in justifying a problematic line of action. Romaioli (2023) develops a dialogical account of the tendency to betray one's good intentions.

text.text: Their question is how such a gap is generated and framed.

The present paper asks how the actor's stance toward the gap changes the observer's evaluation of the actor. Kruger and Gilovich (2004) show that people give themselves more credit for their intentions than they give others for theirs.
text.formatted: The present paper asks how the actor's stance toward the gap changes the observer's evaluation of the actor. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Kruger and Gilovich (2004)</ref> show that people give themselves more credit for their intentions than they give others for theirs.

text.text: Observers therefore weigh an unacted intention lightly.
This is a finding about how much an intention counts.
It does not address how the actor's stance toward the unacted intention changes the observer's evaluation.
The content of a goal also matters to observers. Wingrove and Fitzsimons (2022) studied career, diet, fitness, savings, and academic goals.
text.formatted: The content of a goal also matters to observers. <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Wingrove and Fitzsimons (2022)</ref> studied career, diet, fitness, savings, and academic goals.

text.text: People who conveyed moderately ambitious goals were evaluated most positively.
Highly ambitious and unambitious goals both lowered judgments of warmth and of relationship potential.
This is an effect of what the person aims at.
It leaves open how the person's stance toward an unmet or rejected aim is judged, and its outcome is warmth, where the present question is respect.
Where this stops: the gap is a problem of the actor.
The observer judges intentions and goal content, and stance is left out. Weiner's (1985) attributional theory links the perceived controllability of a cause to emotion.
text.formatted: The observer judges intentions and goal content, and stance is left out. <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Weiner's (1985)</ref> attributional theory links the perceived controllability of a cause to emotion.

Alicke's (2000) culpable control model specifies how observers move from assessments of personal control to blame. Scott and Lyman (1968), building on Mills's (1940) analysis of vocabularies of motive, add the actor's talk.

text.text: An account is a statement made to explain untoward behavior.
Excuses admit that the act was wrong but deny full responsibility.
Justifications accept responsibility but deny that the act was wrong.
The research on excuses that followed is the closest neighbor of the present paper. Weiner et al. (1987) studied excuses for a broken social contract, such as arriving late.
text.formatted: The research on excuses that followed is the closest neighbor of the present paper. <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Weiner et al. (1987)</ref> studied excuses for a broken social contract, such as arriving late.

text.text: Reasons that were external and uncontrollable lessened the anger of the person kept waiting, and internal, controllable reasons increased negative reactions and negative ratings of personality.
A metaanalysis of explanations in organizations found that excuses were more beneficial than justifications (Shaw et al., 2003).
text.formatted: A metaanalysis of explanations in organizations found that excuses were more beneficial than justifications <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Shaw et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: For an obligation to another person, then, a good excuse works. Schlenker et al. (2001), building on the triangle model of responsibility (Schlenker et al., 1994), set out the costs.
text.formatted: For an obligation to another person, then, a good excuse works. <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Schlenker et al. (2001)</ref>, building on the triangle model of responsibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Schlenker et al., 1994)</ref>, set out the costs.

text.text: Excuse-makers risk being seen as deceptive, self-absorbed, and ineffectual, and as unreliable people with flawed character.
Excuses are especially problematic for important, recurring tasks, where they produce long-term disengagement. Steinmetz (2023) brings the question to self-control.
text.formatted: Excuses are especially problematic for important, recurring tasks, where they produce long-term disengagement. <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Steinmetz (2023)</ref> brings the question to self-control.

text.text: A person who failed at a resolution was still perceived to have good selfcontrol when the failure was explained by a lack of money.
A lack of time did not protect the person in the same way, because it was seen as more controllable.
Research on self-handicapping adds the case in which the excuse is offered in advance.
Observers rated the same performance more negatively when it came from a target who made excuses.
A target who claimed low effort also received less favorable feedback than a target who offered no excuse (Rhodewalt et al., 1995).
text.formatted: A target who claimed low effort also received less favorable feedback than a target who offered no excuse <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Rhodewalt et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: In performance settings, then, a controllable cause such as "I did not try" is not rewarded.
This literature establishes that observers judge accounts, that controllability governs the judgment, and that habitual excuse-making damages character.
Three things remain open.
First, its comparisons are among accounts that plead: good and poor excuses, excuses and justifications, excuses and apologies.
Owning in the present sense pleads nothing.
It accepts authorship, offers no mitigating cause, and concedes no wrong.
Second, most of the evidence concerns obligations to others, where the listener was wronged and the account repairs a relationship.
An unmet aspiration of one's own wrongs nobody.
Third, the outcomes are anger, liking, feedback, ability, and perceived self-control.
Respect, contempt, and discounting are not distinguished, so the literature cannot show whether a person can lose on liking or ability and still gain respect.
Where this stops: accounts are ranked by how well they excuse a failure toward others.

The stance of answering for a self-regarding gap without pleading, and its opposite poles, are not theorized. Merton (1938) classifies the ways individuals adapt to culturally prescribed goals, including adaptations that reject the goals.

text.text: Type A is such a case.
Merton's typology concerns the actor's adaptation and its structural sources.
It does not address how others judge a person according to the stance that person takes toward the rejected goal.

Five theories of the actor form the background: agency (Bandura, 2001), self-determination (Ryan & Deci, 2000), self-discrepancy (Higgins, 1987), cognitive dissonance (Festinger, 1957), and self-affirmation (Steele, 1988).

text.text: They explain how actors form, pursue, and protect their aims, and how they experience inconsistency.
They explain why gaps occur and how they feel, and they leave the observer's evaluation open.

The reviewed work supplies the parts: perceived alignment, false signals, two kinds of respect, contempt as an appraisal of character, attribution, the costs of excuses, and akrasia as a social construction.
Three comparisons were not found in the literature searched for this paper.
The first is owning against disowning for a self-regarding aspiration.
The second is respect for a person who owns a shortfall against a conventional goal.
The third is the response to a disowned gap against the response to serial revising.
The next section specifies a construct that makes these tests possible.
>The Construct
text.formatted: <head n="3." >The Construct</head>

text.text: The gap is the distance an observer perceives between an actor's conduct and an aspiration the observer holds the actor to.
The aspiration has one of two sources.
It may be stated by the actor, as in Type B. It may be imputed by convention, as in Type A, where the observer expects the typical aspirations of a person in the actor's position.
Observers interpret others through such typifications (Schutz & Luckmann, 1973), and conventional aspirations for schooling and advancement are among them (Merton, 1938).
text.formatted: Observers interpret others through such typifications <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Schutz & Luckmann, 1973)</ref>, and conventional aspirations for schooling and advancement are among them <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Merton, 1938)</ref>.

text.text: Two points follow.
First, the gap is a perception.
The theory compares stances toward the same perceived gap and needs no metric of its size.
Second, the gap is distinct from attainment.
A person can fail to reach a goal and answer for the distance.
A person can reach a goal through conduct they do not endorse.

The stances are defined as ideal types. Weber (1949) formed ideal types by accentuating selected features of a phenomenon into a consistent picture that no concrete case matches exactly. Etzrodt (2022) argues that consistent derivation is necessary for objectivity but not sufficient, because a consistent interpretation can still be false. Popper's (1959) criterion of falsification supplies the missing step.
text.formatted: The stances are defined as ideal types. <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Weber (1949)</ref> formed ideal types by accentuating selected features of a phenomenon into a consistent picture that no concrete case matches exactly. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Etzrodt (2022)</ref> argues that consistent derivation is necessary for objectivity but not sufficient, because a consistent interpretation can still be false. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Popper's (1959)</ref> criterion of falsification supplies the missing step.

text.text: The paper follows this procedure.
It defines the types, derives propositions from them, and states for each proposition the observation that would refute it.
The types classify stances in an episode, so one person can own one gap and disown another, and can move between stances over time.
The types are derived from a pair of opposites.
Etzrodt (2024a, p. 660) defines Durkheimian anomie as a person's inability to find and realize meaning in life.
Its cause is a lack of regulation or too much freedom.
He defines Marxian alienation, in general terms, as being trapped by one's own creations and unable to develop freely (Etzrodt, 2024a, pp. 659-660).
text.formatted: He defines Marxian alienation, in general terms, as being trapped by one's own creations and unable to develop freely <ref type="bibr">(Etzrodt, 2024a, pp. 659-660)</ref>.

text.text: The two are opposites: anomie is "formless life" and alienation is "lifeless form" (Thom, 1984 , as cited in Etzrodt, 2024a, p. 660).
text.formatted: The two are opposites: anomie is "formless life" and alienation is "lifeless form" <ref type="bibr">(Thom, 1984</ref> <ref type="bibr">, as cited in Etzrodt, 2024a, p. 660)</ref>.

text.text: Read the aspiration as form and conduct as life.
A stated aspiration gives conduct a direction and gives others a standard.
Two questions then generate the types.
Is the aspiration kept?
And does the actor accept authorship of the gap?
When the aspiration is kept and authorship is accepted, the gap is owned.
When the aspiration is given up and authorship is accepted, the actor has made a reflective revision, which is a second form of the owned gap.
When the aspiration is kept and authorship is refused, the gap is disowned.
When aspirations are given up one after another and nobody answers for the change, the gap is dissolved.
The four cells yield three types.
The owned gap (living form).
The actor answers for the distance.
"I have not done it.
That is my choice."
"I said I would, and I did not."
The actor may also revise the aspiration once, on reflection: "I no longer want it."
In each case the word is made to answer for the deed.
Owning requires acknowledgment of authorship and no self-blame.
In the vocabulary of Scott and Lyman (1968), owning is neither an excuse nor an apology.
text.formatted: In the vocabulary of <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Scott and Lyman (1968)</ref>, owning is neither an excuse nor an apology.

text.text: It accepts responsibility as a justification does, but it argues nothing.
The disowned gap (lifeless form).
The actor keeps the aspiration, does not live it, and places its failure outside the self.
"If only I had the time."
"I would have done it, but the timing was bad."
The aspiration is the actor's own creation.
The actor can neither fill it with conduct nor let it go, and treats its failure as the work of outside forces.
In the vocabulary of accounts, disowning is the standing excuse for a recurring task. Schlenker et al. (2001) identify this case as the most damaging to character.
text.formatted: In the vocabulary of accounts, disowning is the standing excuse for a recurring task. <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Schlenker et al. (2001)</ref> identify this case as the most damaging to character.

text.text: This is the alienation pole.
The dissolved gap (formless life).
The actor replaces each aspiration before it is acted on.
This month it is a language, next month a certificate, then a new career.
No aspiration is disowned, because none is kept long enough to fail.
No word holds long enough to bind conduct. Durkheim (1897 Durkheim ( /1951, p. 247, p. 247) tied anomie to desires without limit, which are "insatiable by definition."
text.formatted: No word holds long enough to bind conduct. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Durkheim (1897</ref> <ref type="bibr">Durkheim ( /1951, p. 247, p. 247</ref>) tied anomie to desires without limit, which are "insatiable by definition."

text.text: Serial revising is its everyday form.
This is the anomie pole.
The third type sets a limit on revising.
A single reflective revision belongs to the owned gap, because the actor closes the distance by answering for the change.
Serial revision dissolves the gap without anyone answering for it.

Four neighbors should be kept apart from the construct.
Gap ownership is not self-blame, because a person can own a choice and still name real constraints.
It is not a moral virtue.
A person can own a harmful aim, so the construct describes a mechanism of evaluation and gives no criterion of moral correctness.
It is not achievement, because a person can own a gap and never reach the goal.
And it is not a sequence of stages.
The types are analytical distinctions.
Gap ownership overlaps with false signaling when the actor has made a public claim.
The finding that honest hypocrites are not perceived negatively (Jordan et al., 2017) fits both accounts.
text.formatted: The finding that honest hypocrites are not perceived negatively <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Jordan et al., 2017)</ref> fits both accounts.

text.text: The accounts part where no claim was made.
False signaling treats the speaker as someone who gains, or appears to gain, from a misleading signal.
The present account does not require a strategist.
Etzrodt (2024b) contrasts economic theory, which explains what actors choose, with Schutz, for whom choice is limited by habits and meaning structures.
Disowning talk can be a habit of this kind: a stock excuse in the sense of Scott and Lyman (1968), used without calculation.
Two consequences can be tested.
Disowning should continue where no reputational gain is possible, for example in private talk with intimates who already know the conduct.
And observers should penalize it there as well.
Proposition 3 states the contrast.
Frankfurt (1971) distinguished desires from second-order volitions, in which a person wants a certain desire to be their will.
That distinction concerns the structure of the actor's will.
The present construct concerns what observers infer from talk and conduct, and it requires no claim about the actor's inner hierarchy of desires.

text.text: For a fixed perceived gap, each stance leads the observer to a different inference, and each inference to a different evaluation.
Owning the gap presents the actor as the author of their conduct, including the conduct that falls short.
Authorship is a feature of agency, where admiration responds to merit.
Authorship is therefore a basis for recognition respect in Darwall's (1977) sense.
text.formatted: Authorship is therefore a basis for recognition respect in <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Darwall's (1977)</ref> sense.

text.text: The observer need not share the goal or approve the choice.
The observer treats the person as someone whose conduct is their own and adjusts to that fact.
A neighboring finding supports this step.
Deliberate departures from a norm raise an observer's regard through perceived autonomy, and unintended departures do not (Bellezza et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Deliberate departures from a norm raise an observer's regard through perceived autonomy, and unintended departures do not <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bellezza et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: This explains Type A. The person who says "I do not want more schooling or a promotion" answers for the distance between conventional aspiration and their conduct.
Nobody else is made responsible for it.
The observer recognizes authorship, and respect follows.
Admiration is appraisal respect.
It responds to merit, which here means effort and result.
A person who owns a low aspiration earns recognition respect and no admiration.
This is the dissociation that outcome-based accounts flatten.
It also runs the other way.
A person who reaches a desirable goal under outside pressure can be admired for the result while the observer withholds the respect that authorship earns.
Irritation is the response to a disowned gap.
The actor states the aspiration, does not act, and places the cause outside.
The observer is presented with a distance that nobody answers for and that is not closed by action, by acknowledgment, or by revision.
Irritation is milder than condemnation and more specific than disappointment.
Its object is the open gap.
Contempt appraises character.
Following Fischer and Giner-Sorolla (2016), it arises when character is judged bad and unresponsive to change.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Fischer and Giner-Sorolla (2016)</ref>, it arises when character is judged bad and unresponsive to change.

text.text: Repetition supplies the evidence.
When the same gap is disowned again and again, the stance looks fixed.
The observer then judges a person and no longer an episode: someone who will not act, will not answer, and will not let go.
This is the step from an excuse to a character that Schlenker et al. (2001) describe for recurring tasks.
text.formatted: This is the step from an excuse to a character that <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Schlenker et al. (2001)</ref> describe for recurring tasks.

text.text: This explains Type B. The person who repeatedly announces change and repeatedly explains its absence by circumstances is seen as unresponsive, and contempt follows.
The dissolved gap leads elsewhere.
The serial reviser is highly responsive to change.
Their character cannot be appraised as fixed, so the condition for contempt is absent.
What the observer learns is that the person's stated aspirations do not predict conduct.
The response is discounting: the observer stops treating the person's talk about goals as evidence of what they will do.
Discounting is cooler than contempt.
It withdraws credibility and leaves the person's standing otherwise intact.
The disowner loses credibility as well, since their talk does not predict conduct either.
What separates the two poles is contempt, which needs a stance that looks fixed.
Owning has a limit of the same kind.
An actor who owns the same gap again and again, without acting and without revising, offers words that no longer bind.
Respect is then expected to give way to discounting.
Ownership earns respect while it remains a credible answer.
Two findings fit this account.
People who changed their attitudes were rated as less decisive and less reliable than people whose attitudes stayed stable.
This held even when the change brought them closer to the rater (Allgeier et al., 1979).
text.formatted: This held even when the change brought them closer to the rater <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Allgeier et al., 1979)</ref>.

text.text: The judgment concerns reliability, which is the core of discounting.
And a single disengagement is tolerated.
People who give up a pursuit they were passionate about are judged less harshly than they expect (Berry et al., 2025).
text.formatted: People who give up a pursuit they were passionate about are judged less harshly than they expect <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Berry et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This fits the placement of one reflective revision within the owned gap.
Five other accounts address evaluations in this domain, and they must be separated from ownership.
Misalignment.
On a behavioral integrity account, observers answer the perceived distance between words and deeds as such.
Type A is then respected because word and deed agree, and Type B is penalized because they do not.
No stance is needed.
False signaling.
The actor made a public claim and is seen as holding a favorable image that their conduct does not warrant.
The negative evaluation answers the signal.
The actor complains about the gap to the observer, repeatedly.
The observer bears the cost of listening, and complaining has known interpersonal consequences for those who receive it (Kowalski, 1996).
text.formatted: The observer bears the cost of listening, and complaining has known interpersonal consequences for those who receive it <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kowalski, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: The negative evaluation answers the burden.
The cause named in the account is judged controllable, as with lack of time (Steinmetz, 2023).
text.formatted: The cause named in the account is judged controllable, as with lack of time <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Steinmetz, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The negative evaluation answers a poor excuse, and a better excuse would remove it.
Candor.
Observers may reward honest speech as such, so that "that is my choice" is only the truthful report.
A candor account expects no difference when the disowner's stated cause is also true.
Ownership expects a difference even then, because the stance is judged and not only its accuracy.
The ownership account holds that the stance itself is judged.
Its central test is a matched contrast: the same stated aspiration and the same inaction, with only the account varied.
Misalignment is then equal, so an integrity account expects no difference between "that is my choice" and "if only".
Ownership expects more respect for the first.
It expects an owned gap, which names a fully controllable cause, to earn more respect than a disowned gap with a plausible excuse.
A controllability account expects the opposite, and the evidence from performance settings is on its side (Rhodewalt et al., 1995; Steinmetz, 2023).
text.formatted: A controllability account expects the opposite, and the evidence from performance settings is on its side <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Rhodewalt et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Steinmetz, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The ownership prediction therefore runs against the usual result.
It concerns a different outcome.
The owner may be judged lower in self-control or effort and still be respected more.
It expects the penalty for disowning where no claim was made and where the observer is a bystander who bears no cost.
It treats a prior claim and listener burden as amplifiers.
Section 5 sets out where the accounts make different predictions.
>Propositions, Rival Predictions, and Boundary Conditions

text.text: Table 2.
Propositions and the observations that would refute them Proposition Refuted if P1.
Desirability independence For a fixed gap in a self-regarding aspiration, an owned stance earns more respect than a disowned stance, whether the aspiration is conventionally desirable or not.
Desirability may still affect liking.
The effect of ownership on respect appears only for desirable aspirations, or the desirability of the aspiration accounts for the difference in respect.
Respect without admiration An owned shortfall against a conventional goal yields recognition respect without admiration.
Respect and admiration rise and fall together across all conditions.
Beyond false signaling The effect of ownership holds when the actor made no public claim and no reputational gain is possible.
The effect is absent whenever no claim was made.
Ownership is then a case of false signaling.
Repetition Contempt rises with repeated disowning of the same gap and falls after a single reflective revision.
Repeated owning without action draws discounting.
Contempt does not depend on repetition, or a single revision does not lower it, or repeated owning keeps its full respect.
Burden Disowning is judged more harshly when the observer bears the cost of hearing it.
Harshness is the same for listeners and bystanders.
(A penalty that disappears entirely for bystanders refutes P3, since burden would then be the cause.)
Discounting Serial revising draws discounting and not contempt.
Serial revisers are held in the same contempt as repeated disowners.
Domain For a self-regarding aspiration, owning earns more respect than a plausible excuse, even where the excuse protects perceived self-control.
For an obligation to another person, the plausible excuse does at least as well as owning.
A plausible excuse earns as much respect as owning for self-regarding aspirations, or owning beats the excuse equally in both domains.

Three further contrasts complete the set.
The matched contrast described in Section 4.6 separates ownership from behavioral integrity.
The second separates ownership from a controllability account of excuses.
The third separates it from candor: the disowned account names a cause that the observer knows to be true.
For a self-regarding aspiration, compare an owned gap ("I chose not to") with a disowned gap that names a plausible, uncontrollable cause.
Controllability predicts more favorable judgment of the excuse.
Ownership predicts more respect for the owned gap (P7).
The first row does not separate the accounts.
The second and third rows are decisive for ownership against both rivals.
If the effect of ownership appears without a claim and for a bystander, false signaling and burden are each insufficient.
If it does not, the ownership account reduces to one of them.
Visible constraints.
Economic, institutional, and health constraints can prevent conduct.
When the observer can see the constraint, naming it is an accurate report.
Observers who perceive the constraint are predicted to withhold the disowning inference.
This agrees with the finding that a less controllable cause preserves the image of self-control (Steinmetz, 2023).

text.text: Whose aspiration it was.
If an aspiration was adopted to satisfy family expectations, failing to enact it does not show a disowned gap.
The stated aspiration was never the actor's own.
An actor who says so owns the gap.
Commitments that others rely on.
The tolerance for one reflective revision is predicted for selfregarding aspirations.
Where others depend on a commitment, changing course has a cost.
Decision makers who escalated commitment were perceived as more trustworthy than those who did not (Dorison et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Decision makers who escalated commitment were perceived as more trustworthy than those who did not <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dorison et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Leaders who changed a moral stance were seen as hypocritical (Kreps et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Leaders who changed a moral stance were seen as hypocritical <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Kreps et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Time.
Some aspirations take long to show in conduct.
The disowning inference requires that the observer has seen enough time pass.
Observability.
Observers often know little of the actor's conduct and constraints.
Perceived stance is a judgment under uncertainty.
Culture.
Condemnation of word-deed misalignment is weaker in interdependent cultural contexts (Effron et al., 2018a).
text.formatted: Condemnation of word-deed misalignment is weaker in interdependent cultural contexts <ref type="bibr">(Effron et al., 2018a)</ref>.

text.text: The rules that link stance to evaluation may vary in the same way.
The propositions should be tested in at least two cultural contexts.
>Discussion
text.formatted: <head n="6." >Discussion</head>

text.text: The paper speaks to five literatures.
Word-deed misalignment.
The paper extends the analysis from moral standing to self-regarding aspirations and names the actor's stance as a construct with types.
In the existing studies, acknowledgment is an experimental condition.
Here it is the variable of interest, and its opposite has two forms.
The paper adds a stance that the account typologies do not contain: answering for a gap without pleading.
It also predicts a reversal by domain.
Where someone was wronged, a good excuse repairs the relationship.
Where the aspiration was the actor's own, there is nothing to repair, and the excuse only shows that the actor does not answer for their conduct.
Anomie and alienation.
Etzrodt (2024a) set the pair as opposites at the level of rationalization processes.
This paper applies it at the level of one person's aspiration and conduct.
Observers are expected to answer the two poles differently, with contempt for lifeless form and discounting for formless life.
The framework explains how observers evaluate, and it ranks no way of living above another.
Ownership earns recognition respect for agency, and an observer can grant that respect while condemning the aim on moral grounds.
The two judgments are distinct and can coexist.
The demand to own a gap is itself a social expectation, and it may not fall equally on everyone.
"I have no time" can be heard as an accurate report from a night-shift worker with two jobs and as an excuse from a salaried professional.
The design below can test this by varying the actor's occupation.
The construct is perceptual, and Section 5.3 marks the conditions under which talk is not read as stance.
Perceived ownership has three close neighbors, perceived integrity, authenticity, and honesty.
The matched contrast and the second and third rows of Table 3 show whether it predicts respect beyond them.
text.formatted: The matched contrast and the second and third rows of Table <ref type="table">3</ref> show whether it predicts respect beyond them.

text.text: The framework changes what an account is expected to do.
Take a colleague who has said for a year that they will apply for a promotion and has not applied.
"The timing was never right" protects the moment and, repeated, costs character.
"I decided I did not want it enough" may cost some liking and still earn respect.
For research on excuses, this means that liking, perceived selfcontrol, and respect should be measured separately, because the accounts that protect one may lose another.
The propositions can be tested with vignettes.
The core design crosses stance (owned, disowned, dissolved) with the desirability of the aspiration (desirable, not desirable) and with prior public claim (made, not made).
A domain factor (an aspiration of one's own, an obligation to another person) and a disowned condition with a plausible, uncontrollable cause test P7.
The gap is held fixed within each comparison: the same aspiration and the same conduct, with only the actor's talk varied.
One vignette illustrates the three stances.
In January a colleague says they will study for an accounting certificate.
By June they have not opened the book.
Asked about it, they answer in one of three ways.
Owned: "I have not done it.
I chose to spend my evenings on other things."
Disowned: "I would have, but work has been impossible."
Dissolved: "I am over that.
Now I am going to learn Spanish."
Outcomes are recognition respect, admiration, irritation, contempt, and discounting.

Illustrative items are "This person is entitled to decide this for themselves" for recognition respect (worded to stay apart from credibility, which the discounting measure covers), "I look up to what this person has achieved" for admiration, and "I look down on this person" for contempt.
Discounting is measured as the predicted likelihood that the actor's next stated aspiration will be acted on.
Observer position (listener, bystander) tests P5, and the number of episodes (one, three) tests P4.
Perceived gap size and the perceived controllability of the cause are measured as manipulation checks, so that stance can be separated from both.
Perceived integrity, authenticity, and honesty are measured as covariates.
Running the design in Japan and in the United States tests the cultural boundary, since condemnation of word-deed misalignment differed between these two countries (Effron et al., 2018a).
text.formatted: Running the design in Japan and in the United States tests the cultural boundary, since condemnation of word-deed misalignment differed between these two countries <ref type="bibr">(Effron et al., 2018a)</ref>.

text.text: Return to the two cases.
The first person says plainly that they do not want more schooling or a promotion.
They are respected because they answer for the distance between conventional aspiration and their conduct.
The second person keeps saying they will study, get fit, and change, and never does.
They are held in contempt because they keep the aspiration, do not live it, and place its failure outside themselves.
A third person, who replaces each aspiration before acting on it, is neither respected nor despised, because their talk stops counting.
Observers judge how people stand toward the distance between what they are held to and what they do, more than what they choose.

The paper names a cue for recognition respect in everyday talk, which Darwall's normative distinction leaves open.
The cue is a plain statement of authorship offered without a plea, such as "I have not done it, and that is my choice."
